output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation reveals a severe multi-domain amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of episodic memory. Verbal learning is severely impaired (HVLT-R total learning 3rd percentile) with near-absent delayed recall (1/12, <1st percentile) and a near-chance recognition discrimination index, consistent with a profound storage-type memory deficit with limited cueing benefit. output.query: rapidly progressive Alzheimer's disease versus Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease differential diagnosis biomarkers

results.authors: Schmidt C, Wolff M, Weitz M, et al.
results.summary: Describes rpAD as a distinct clinical entity comprising approximately 10-15% of all prion-surveillance referrals. rpAD is defined by cognitive decline progressing to severe dementia within 1-2 years of symptom onset. CSF biomarkers (reduced Abeta42, elevated p-tau) and positive amyloid PET distinguish rpAD from sCJD; 14-3-3 protein and RT-QuIC are key exclusionary tests for prion disease. DWI restriction in the cortex (ribboning) or basal ganglia strongly supports CJD over rpAD.
results.title: Rapidly progressive neurodegenerative dementia: a rare entity or an underdiagnosed clinical variant?

results.authors: Ladogana A, Sanchez-Juan P, Mitrova E, et al.
results.summary: Systematic neuropathological and clinical series distinguishing rpAD from sCJD. Hallmarks favoring rpAD over CJD: amnestic-predominant onset, absent myoclonus, no periodic discharges on EEG, no cortical ribboning on DWI, and a high CSF p-tau/total-tau ratio exceeding typical prion thresholds. RT-QuIC specificity exceeds 99% for prion disease in CSF.
results.title: Clinical and biomarker characterization of rapidly progressive neurodegenerative dementia

results.authors: Geschwind MD, Shu H, Haman A, et al.
results.summary: Prospective series of 178 patients referred for possible CJD: 40% proved to have non-prion etiologies. Among confirmed non-prion diagnoses, Alzheimer's disease (including rpAD) was the most common neurodegenerative mimic. Key discriminators: myoclonus, periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, and DWI cortical ribboning/basal-ganglia restriction together identify CJD with >90% sensitivity; their absence, combined with AD biomarker positivity, supports rpAD.
results.title: Evaluation of rapidly progressive dementia: Diagnostic approach and common etiologies

prohibited_recommendations: Do not label the diagnosis as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease based solely on the rapid tempo of cognitive decline without confirmation by RT-QuIC, DWI, or EEG
Do not stop the Alzheimer's disease biomarker workup because the decline is rapid — rpAD is a recognized entity and confirmed neurodegenerative pathology can coexist with an accelerated course
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in Alzheimer's disease
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of behavioral symptoms given fall risk and cognitive worsening
Do not attribute the cognitive decline to diabetes alone; suboptimally controlled T2DM is a risk modifier but cannot explain a rapidly progressive amnestic dementia syndrome
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant, specifically documenting the tempo of decline and explicitly inquiring about myoclonus, seizures, visual changes, and behavioral disturbance
Perform dedicated DWI/ADC MRI sequences with attention to cortical ribboning and basal-ganglia restriction before concluding prion disease is absent
Order CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 protein alongside AD biomarkers (Abeta42, p-tau, total tau) to simultaneously exclude prion disease and confirm neurodegenerative pathology
Exclude reversible causes of rapid cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate)
Do NOT accept the rapid tempo alone as evidence of CJD — establish the absence of CJD hallmarks (myoclonus, PSWCs on EEG, DWI ribboning, positive RT-QuIC) before narrowing to rpAD
Assess patient safety: driving cessation, medication management, and caregiver support needs given severity of impairment
Disclose diagnosis and discuss prognosis with patient and family including the possibility of a more rapid disease trajectory than typical AD

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom, syncope, or arrhythmia to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this rapidly progressive cognitive presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI with DWI is available and has already been performed; MRI is the preferred and more sensitive modality for this workup
DaTscan evaluates dopaminergic system integrity for parkinsonism; no parkinsonism, tremor, or DLB features are present in this case

differential.key_features: Rapid decline tempo mimics CJD; excluded here by absent myoclonus, no periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, no DWI cortical ribboning or basal-ganglia restriction, negative 14-3-3, and negative RT-QuIC

Subacute rapidly progressive amnestic syndrome can reflect autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2, anti-NMDAR); workup should consider serum/CSF neural antibody panel if AD biomarkers are inconclusive
Subacute dementia with rapid progression warrants paraneoplastic evaluation; no known malignancy and no systemic B-symptoms in this patient argue against it

differential.diagnosis: Frontotemporal dementia (behavioral variant or semantic variant)
differential.key_features: Predominantly amnestic profile with hippocampal atrophy and positive AD biomarkers argues against FTD; disinhibition or semantic loss would be more prominent in FTD
Shares the same biomarker profile as typical AD but is distinguished by tempo — rapid functional decline over 6-8 months is atypical for the usual 3-5 year course of early-stage AD

differential.diagnosis: Vascular or toxic-metabolic rapid cognitive decline
differential.key_features: Suboptimally controlled diabetes is a vascular risk factor, but DWI shows no acute infarcts, and the progressive amnestic course with positive AD biomarkers is inconsistent with a purely vascular or metabolic etiology

key_clinical_evidence: Rapidly progressive Alzheimer's disease (rpAD) is a recognized phenotypic variant in which decline progresses to severe dementia within 1-2 years; the clinical tempo that prompts a CJD referral does not, by itself, exclude AD

The CJD hallmarks of myoclonus, periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, and DWI cortical ribboning or basal-ganglia restriction are all absent here — their absence substantially lowers the prior probability of prion disease
Negative RT-QuIC in CSF has specificity exceeding 99% for ruling out sporadic CJD; negative 14-3-3 provides additional supporting evidence against prion disease

The CSF A+T+ profile (reduced Abeta42/40 ratio, elevated p-tau-181, elevated total tau) is inconsistent with CJD and confirms the AD pathological process; markedly elevated total tau in the context of A+T+ profile is seen in both CJD and rpAD but is distinguished by RT-QuIC and DWI
Positive amyloid PET provides definitive evidence of amyloid pathology (not expected in CJD) and closes the differential

The predominant amnestic phenotype with hippocampal atrophy on MRI and multi-domain neuropsychological impairment characteristic of a storage-type (hippocampal-driven) memory deficit is the signature of AD, not CJD

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Rapid tempo alone cannot distinguish rpAD from CJD; the discriminating evidence lies in the absence of myoclonus, PSWCs, and DWI ribboning, combined with a positive AD biomarker profile and negative RT-QuIC
red_herrings.data_point: Rapid cognitive decline over 6-8 months prompting urgent referral to 'exclude CJD' by the primary care physician
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchored on tempo may commit to CJD as the leading diagnosis before systematically assessing CJD-specific hallmarks and AD biomarkers

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated total tau is a non-specific marker of neuronal injury seen in both CJD and severe AD; its discrimination requires concurrent RT-QuIC, p-tau profile, and DWI assessment — the A+T+ pattern with negative RT-QuIC here points to rpAD, not CJD
red_herrings.data_point: Elevated total tau in CSF (612 pg/mL, reference <400 pg/mL)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Markedly elevated total tau may be misread as a prion disease marker supporting CJD, particularly in the context of a rapid course

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Rapidly progressive amnestic Alzheimer's disease where the rate of decline has triggered an urgent CJD referral; the agent must systematically assess and exclude CJD hallmarks while confirming AD biomarker positivity
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the reviewed cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Biomarker route: required CSF Alzheimer and prion assays, with no duplicate CSF/PET confirmation. Case-specific additions: optional EEG for periodic complexes in the CJD differential.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of rpAD as a distinct AD phenotype; distinguishes it from CJD through systematic evaluation of EEG, DWI, and CSF prion markers; illustrates that rapid tempo alone does not mandate a prion diagnosis
key_educational_points: Rapidly progressive Alzheimer's disease is an underdiagnosed clinical variant presenting with dementia over months rather than years
CJD should be excluded via RT-QuIC, DWI cortical ribboning assessment, and EEG periodic discharges before narrowing to rpAD
Negative RT-QuIC has >99% specificity for excluding sporadic CJD and is the most reliable single exclusionary test
Elevated total tau is non-specific and can be markedly elevated in both CJD and rpAD; discrimination requires the full biomarker and imaging panel
Absent myoclonus, absent PSWCs on EEG, and absent DWI cortical ribboning together substantially lower the probability of CJD
This case exposes required CSF Alzheimer and prion assays as its only biomarker route; conclusive CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET must not be ordered together
metadata.real_seed_note: Case demographics and clinical scenario are loosely modeled on published descriptions of rpAD cohorts presenting with CJD-in-differential workups (e.g., Schmidt et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2011; Geschwind et al., Ann Neurol 2008). A specific PMC case report with CC-BY license of confirmed rpAD with CJD exclusion was not identified at the time of authoring; this case is an authentic de novo rpAD construction following the RP-subtype policy. PMC literature search was performed; no single verifiable CC-BY case report meeting all inclusion criteria (confirmed rpAD, CJD excluded by RT-QuIC, positive AD biomarkers) was found.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Pearson is a 68-year-old right-handed retired chemistry teacher referred urgently to the neurology memory clinic by his primary care physician for evaluation of rapidly progressive cognitive decline. His wife, Ruth, provides the majority of the history. Approximately 8 months ago, Mr. Pearson began forgetting names of colleagues he had known for decades and misplacing personal items daily. His wife initially attributed this to stress and the adjustment to retirement. Over the following 2 months, however, his memory deterioration accelerated markedly. He began forgetting conversations he had had hours earlier, asking the same questions repeatedly within a single sitting, and failing to recognize that he had already eaten a meal an hour before. By 5 months ago, he was unable to follow recipes he had previously made from memory, could not operate the television remote without step-by-step guidance, and became disoriented within the familiar neighborhood where he has lived for 24 years. He stopped driving 4 months ago after twice becoming disoriented on routes he knew well. His wife describes the tempo as 'shockingly fast' — 'within six months he went from forgetting names to not knowing where he was.' She consulted his primary care physician, who found an MMSE of 22 at that visit. Over the subsequent 2 months MMSE declined to 18. His primary care physician, alarmed by the rate of decline, searched the internet, read about Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and made an urgent neurology referral with a letter explicitly requesting 'CJD evaluation.' There have been NO witnessed myoclonic jerks, no seizure-like episodes, no bizarre dreams or acting-out behaviors, and no visual hallucinations at any point. His wife expressly denies any 'jerking movements.' His sleep is reported as unremarkable by his wife. He has not had fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, or any new neurological symptoms suggesting a systemic illness. He has no history of neurosurgical procedures, blood transfusions, or dural exposure. He has not consumed wild game or unusual animal products. He has had no recent international travel. There is no family history of prion disease. His mood has been flat and he has been increasingly withdrawn, but he denies being depressed when directly asked. He remains ambulatory without assistance and maintains continence.

neurological_exam.additional: No myoclonus. No asterixis. No alien limb phenomenon. No paratonic rigidity. Go/no-go testing: 2 of 10 errors (mildly impaired inhibitory control). Frontal release signs: bilateral palmomental reflexes present; no snout reflex; grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally. No dysdiadochokinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact and conjugate; no nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Facial movement symmetric. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline, no fasciculations. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait mildly uncertain but no frank ataxia. Romberg negative. No postural instability on gentle pull-test. No shuffling, freezing, or festination.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person; oriented to city but cannot identify the hospital by name. States the year correctly but cannot identify the month or date. MMSE 18/30 — lost 4 points on orientation (month, date, building, floor), 3 points on recall (0/3 words at 5 minutes, 0 with category cues), 2 on serial sevens (cannot continue past first subtraction), 1 on sentence repetition, 1 on writing (produces a single fragmented phrase). MoCA 13/30 with severe deficits in delayed recall (0/5, 0 recovered with category cues), trail-making (errors on alternating sequence), visuospatial (clock drawing — numbers spaced asymmetrically, hands placed incorrectly), abstraction (0/2), and naming (misnames 'rhinoceros' and hesitates on 'lion'). Verbal fluency: 6 animals in 60 seconds; 4 F-words in 60 seconds. His wife describes the decline as occurring over the past 6-8 months and notes 'he went from not quite himself to needing help with the remote control in just a few months.' No paranoid ideation or formed hallucinations reported.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal muscle bulk. Tone normal throughout — no cogwheel rigidity, no lead-pipe rigidity. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor at rest or with action. No myoclonus elicited by startle, arm extension, or percussion of wrists.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. Mild bilateral palmomental reflexes present. No grasp reflex elicited.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation intact throughout all extremities. Vibration sense reduced at the bilateral great toes but intact at the ankles. Proprioception intact. No cortical sensory deficits tested (graphesthesia, stereognosis not formally assessed but informal bedside testing intact).
